687.howItsDone: In Maharashtra, Karnataka and nearby regions, the day after the main Diwali night is kept as Bali Pratipada, honoring King Bali's yearly return; in many places it is also a new-year day and a day of gifts between husbands and wives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri's tenth day, Ravana burned, Durga sent home, first letters in rice. shakti: even rama bowed to the goddess first.

segments.voice: Diwali has a morning after. The Lakshmi night is done, and in Maharashtra and Karnataka families light lamps again, this time for a king coming home. Not Rama. Bali, a demon king, an asura, the one the gods defeated. In Maharashtra some say a line that goes, roughly: let troubles go, and let Bali's kingdom come. So why would anyone light lamps for a demon? Because of how he lost.
screen: `THE MORNING AFTER THE LAKSHMI NIGHT.` → `A KING COMES BACK.` → `A DEMON KING.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. Bali, grandson of Prahlad, the boy from the Holi fire, has grown so powerful and so generous that he rules all three worlds, and the gods have lost their places. Vishnu comes to restore the balance as Vamana, a small boy, a young brahmin student with an umbrella and a water pot, at a great sacrifice Bali is holding. Bali is known for never refusing a guest. Ask for anything, he says. The boy asks for three steps of land, measured by his own feet. Bali laughs: ask for more. But Bali's teacher, Shukra, sees through it and warns him: this is Vishnu, and he'll take everything. Bali gives anyway. I promised, he says, and I won't take back my word. Then the boy grows. One step covers the earth, the second the heavens, and there's nowhere left for the third. So Bali bows and offers his own head. Vishnu sends him down to a lower realm, Sutala, but praises his truthfulness and promises to stand guard at his door himself. That's the teaching under the lamps. In Hindu stories, the side you're born on doesn't settle who is good. Bali is an asura, and so was Prahlad, and the Bhagavata names both among the Lord's great devotees. What it honors is satya, truthfulness, and dana, giving, kept even when they cost a kingdom. So on Bali Pratipada, a family lighting a lamp at the door is honoring a king for what he did, not for where he came from.

688.title: Holi: the Lord in the pillar
688.hook: Prahlad says the Lord is even in a stone pillar; his father strikes it, and Narasimha bursts out

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali and King Bali, a demon king honored for keeping his word, who comes home once a year.
screen: `A KING WHO KEPT HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: At the Holi bonfire, Prahlad walks out of the fire. But the story doesn't stop there, and the Bhagavata Purana carries it further. His father, the king Hiranyakashipu, has tried everything to kill him, and nothing works. Finally, in a rage, he stands before his son in the great hall and asks: this Vishnu of yours, who you say is everywhere. Is he in this pillar? The boy says yes. And the king strikes the pillar.
screen: `THE FIRE WAS NOT THE END.` → `IS HE IN THIS PILLAR?` → `THE KING STRIKES IT.`

segments.voice: To understand what happens next, you need the king's boon. Long before, after fierce austerities, Hiranyakashipu had been granted protection, as the Bhagavata tells it, with a long list of conditions. No man or animal could kill him. Not by day or by night. Not inside or outside. Not on the earth or in the sky. Not with any weapon. He thought he'd closed every door. When he strikes the pillar, it splits open, and out comes Narasimha: Vishnu as half man, half lion. Neither man nor animal. He seizes the king at twilight, neither day nor night; on the threshold of the hall, neither inside nor outside; across his lap, neither earth nor sky; and ends him with his claws, which are not a weapon. Narasimha's fury is so terrible that even the gods are afraid to come near. They send the boy. Prahlad bows, and Narasimha calms and puts his hand on his head. Offered any blessing, Prahlad asks that his father, who tried to kill him again and again, be purified and freed, and the Bhagavata says it is granted. Under the whole story sits one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the Lord isn't only in the temple or in heaven. He is in everything, so fully that he can step out of a stone column. Many teachers read Prahlad's wish the same way: if the Lord is in everyone, he is in the father who hurt him too. That's why Holi's fire is for Prahlad, and its morning is for visiting, making up, and putting color on old rivals as well as friends.

Then, for one breath, wish them free of whatever made them act that way. If you pray, say it to Narasimha. Let it go with the out-breath.

689.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
689.hook: two gods race to find the end of a pillar of fire; why the lingam is a sign, and why Shivaratri is kept awake
689.carry: the lingam: a sign of what has no end
689.tomorrow: Rantideva's last cup: whose is wealth?
689.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Shiva temples and households divide the night into four watches and bathe the lingam in each, with water, milk, curd, ghee or honey, chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn; Lingodbhava images often appear on the western wall of South Indian Shiva temples.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, Narasimha from the pillar, and Prahlad asking for his father's release. The Lord is in the pillar, and in everyone.
screen: `NOT REVENGE, BUT RELEASE.`

segments.voice: Two gods are arguing about which of them is greater: Brahma, the creator, and Vishnu, the preserver. It's getting heated. Then, between them, a column of fire appears, with no visible top and no visible bottom. It just goes up and down, beyond seeing. The argument stops. This is one of the best-known stories told about why the lingam is worshiped, and why some people keep Shivaratri awake all night.
screen: `BRAHMA AND VISHNU ARGUE.` → `A COLUMN OF FIRE APPEARS.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, and it's called the Lingodbhava, the appearance of the lingam. The two gods agree: whoever finds an end of the pillar is the greater. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs downward. Brahma becomes a swan and flies upward. They go for ages, and neither finds an end. Vishnu comes back and says honestly: I couldn't find it. Brahma, in many tellings, claims he did, and is caught in the lie. Then Shiva appears from inside the pillar of fire, and in the Shaiva telling, both gods bow to something with no edges at all. That's the teaching in the lingam. Linga means a sign, a mark. For Shaivas, Shiva is the one beyond every measure, and the lingam is a sign of that, not a statue of a face, because any face would be too small. Many Shaivas say Maha Shivaratri is the night that pillar appeared. So the night is divided into four watches, called praharas, roughly three hours each. In many temples and homes there's an abhisheka in each watch, the lingam bathed again, often with a different offering each time: milk, curd, ghee, honey, and always water. In between, the five syllables: na, mah, shi, va, ya. Om Namah Shivaya. Staying awake is part of the offering: for one night, the endless matters more than sleep. And with that, the festival days are done. Tomorrow, a king who gives away his last cup of water.
screen: `LINGODBHAVA: THE PILLAR OF FIRE.` · `NEITHER GOD FINDS AN END.` · `LINGA: A SIGN, NOT A FACE.` · `FOUR WATCHES, FOUR BATHS.` · then, large: `A SIGN OF WHAT HAS NO END.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya silently, once with each breath, the way the vigil does through the night. If not, follow one breath all the way in, looking for where it begins, and all the way out, looking for where it ends. Neither god found the pillar's end, and you may not find an edge either. When you want to stop, stay three breaths longer.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, kept in four watches, and remembered by many as the night the pillar of fire appeared, with no end either way.

690.title: Rantideva's last cup: whose is wealth?
690.hook: a starving king gives his last food and water to guests, and the Isha's first verse asks whose wealth it is anyway
690.carry: it's all the lord's: enjoy it, don't grab
690.tomorrow: Arjuna drops his bow: work that doesn't cling

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, and the lingam, a sign of what has no end. Now the festivals are done, and three days begin on karma, the way of action.
screen: `A SIGN OF WHAT HAS NO END.`

segments.voice: A king hasn't eaten in forty-eight days. Not for a vow: he has given everything away, and his family has gone hungry with him. On the forty-ninth morning, food and water arrive. He's about to eat when there's a knock. A guest. Then another. Then another. A short Upanishad asks the question his story answers: whose, after all, is anything you own?
screen: `FORTY-EIGHT DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` → `A MEAL ARRIVES.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its ninth book. King Rantideva sees the Lord in every being, so he gives a share to the first guest, a brahmin. Then a laborer comes, and he gives again. Then a man with a pack of hungry dogs, and he gives the rest of the food. Only the water is left, and an outcaste comes begging for a drink. Rantideva is dying of thirst himself. He gives it, and says, roughly: I don't ask for powers, or even for freedom from rebirth; let me take on the pain of every being, so they're free of it. Then the guests show themselves: they were the gods, come to test him. He asks them for nothing. Now hear the Isha Upanishad's first verse beside him. Isha vasyam idam sarvam: all this, whatever moves in this moving world, is dwelt in by the Lord. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: enjoy by letting go, or, in another reading, enjoy what has been given. Ma gridhah: do not covet. Kasya svid dhanam: whose, after all, is wealth? That's the Hindu teaching under karma, the way of action: what you have isn't finally yours. It's the Lord's, lent to you. Shankara hears renunciation in the verse; others hear gratitude. Rantideva is the extreme case. The everyday case is in many Hindu kitchens: food is offered to God first, and only then eaten, as prasad, a gift given back. Gandhi is reported to have said that if every other scripture were lost and only this verse survived, Hinduism would still live.
screen: `RANTIDEVA GIVES TO EVERY GUEST.` · `HIS LAST WATER, TO AN OUTCASTE.` · `ALL THIS IS DWELT IN BY THE LORD.` · `DON'T COVET. WHOSE IS WEALTH?` · then, large: `IT'S ALL THE LORD'S: ENJOY, DON'T GRAB.`

segments.voice: At your next meal, do what many Hindu homes do: pause with the plate before you eat. If you pray, offer it silently to God, in any words. If you don't, think of everyone and everything that made it. Either way, say to yourself the verse's question, whose is this, really? Then eat it slowly, as a gift.

691.title: Arjuna drops his bow: work that doesn't cling
691.hook: Arjuna drops his bow and says he'd rather beg; Krishna and the Isha both say keep working, and offer the fruit
691.carry: karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit
691.tomorrow: Ajamila's last word: the name at the end

screen: `IT'S ALL THE LORD'S: ENJOY, DON'T GRAB.`

segments.voice: On the morning of the great battle, Arjuna, the finest archer alive, looks across the field and sees his teachers, his cousins, his grandfather. His bow slips from his hand. Better, he says, to live on alms in this world than to do this. He's ready to quit, and to call quitting the holy choice. His charioteer is Krishna. And Krishna says no.
screen: `THE MORNING OF THE BATTLE.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.` → `KRISHNA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer, in the Bhagavad Gita, isn't fight because you'll win. It's stranger. No one, he says, can stay even a moment without acting. So the question isn't whether to act, but how. Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Don't make the fruit your motive, and don't cling to not acting either. He names a king who lived it: Janaka and others reached perfection through action itself. And he gives an image: whoever acts, offering the work to the Lord and letting go of clinging, is no more stained by wrong than a lotus leaf by water. That's karma yoga, the yoga of action: do your part fully, and offer what comes of it. The Isha Upanishad says it in a single line. Verse two: kurvann eveha karmani, doing works here, jijivishet shatam samah, one may wish to live a hundred years. Then: na karma lipyate nare. Action does not cling to the person. Lipyate means smeared on, sticking, the same verb the Gita uses for the lotus leaf. Shankara reads the Isha's verse as a concession for those not yet ready to renounce; other teachers hear it as a full path in itself. Either way, the tradition doesn't ask a busy person to leave. It asks them to change the grip: the work is yours to do well, and the result is offered. That's why many Hindus offer their work before they start it, a short prayer before study, a book touched to the forehead, tools honored once a year at Ayudha Puja.

692.title: Ajamila's last word: the name at the end
692.hook: dying and afraid, Ajamila calls his son's name, Narayana, and the Lord's messengers come; the Isha's last verses ask the mind to remember
692.carry: smarana: keep the lord's name close
692.howItsDone: Many Hindu families chant the Lord's name, or play recitations, beside someone who is dying, and in many North Indian funeral processions mourners call 'Ram naam satya hai', the name of Ram is truth. Many keep the name close every day through japa.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's dropped bow, and the Isha's second verse. Karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit.
screen: `DO THE WORK. OFFER THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: An old man is dying, and he's afraid. He's eighty-eight, and he has spent most of his life gambling, cheating and stealing to keep his family fed. Now he sees three terrible figures with ropes, the messengers of Yama, lord of death, come to drag him away. His youngest son is playing a little way off. The old man calls out to him by name. And the boy's name is Narayana.
screen: `AN OLD MAN, DYING, AFRAID.` → `YAMA'S MESSENGERS, WITH ROPES.` → `HE CALLS: NARAYANA!`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its sixth book. Ajamila had once been a careful young brahmin, before he fell into a very different life. But Narayana is also a name of Vishnu, and when he cries it out, Vishnu's own messengers appear and stop Yama's. An argument follows about dharma and deeds, and Vishnu's messengers win it: the Lord's name, said even to call a child, even without meaning it, reaches further than a lifetime of wrongs. Ajamila is given more life. He goes to the Ganges at Haridwar, gives himself to devotion, and at the end goes with the Lord's messengers. Now set beside him the Isha Upanishad's last verses, which Shankara hears as the words of someone at the end of life. Let the breath go to the wind; let this body end in ashes. Then: Om. Mind, remember. Remember what was done. Said twice. The last verse asks Agni, the fire, to lead by a good path; it also appears in the Rig Veda. Two Hindu answers to the last moment, and they meet. The Isha, as many read it, asks for an honest look at your karma, everything you did. The Bhagavata says the Lord's name can carry you further still. That's the teaching of smarana, remembering: keep the Lord's name close every day, so it's what the mind reaches for when it matters. Krishna says it in the Gita: whoever leaves the body remembering me comes to me. It's why families chant the name beside someone who is dying, and why some people say Ram, Ram, every night before sleep.
screen: `VISHNU'S MESSENGERS STOP YAMA'S.` · `THE NAME REACHES FURTHER THAN WRONGS.` · `OM. MIND, REMEMBER WHAT WAS DONE.` · `SMARANA: KEEP THE NAME CLOSE.` · then, large: `THE NAME AT THE END.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one name of God, the one your family uses, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, and say it slowly, once with each breath, ten times. If you don't, choose a word that holds what you love most. Then do what the Isha asks, gently: remember what was done today, without grading any of it. End with the name once more.
Karma. Action, everything a person did. At the end, the Isha asks the mind to remember it; the Bhagavata says the Lord's name reaches further still.

693.title: Narada's glimpse: bhakti, supreme love
693.hook: a servant's boy hears the sages' stories, glimpses the Lord once, and spends his life singing; the sutras credited to him call it supreme love
693.carry: bhakti: supreme love that wants nothing else
693.howItsDone: Some Hindus, especially in Vaishnava communities, study the Narada Bhakti Sutras in satsang groups, reading a few sutras and a commentary together. Bhakti itself is lived in puja, kirtan, japa and service offered to a chosen form of God.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ajamila's last word, the Isha's last verses, and the end of three days on karma. Smarana: keep the Lord's name close.
screen: `THE NAME AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Long before he was the wandering sage with the vina, Narada says, he was a servant's little boy. One rainy season, a group of wandering sages stayed where his mother worked. The boy served them, ate what they left with their blessing, and listened while they told stories of Krishna, every day, for months. Something in him turned toward what he heard. Then the sages moved on.
screen: `A SERVANT'S LITTLE BOY.` → `THE SAGES' STORIES, ALL SEASON.` → `SOMETHING IN HIM TURNS.`

segments.voice: Narada tells this himself, to Vyasa, in the first book of the Bhagavata Purana. Not long after, his mother died, bitten by a snake, and the boy, with no one left, walked north. In a forest, under a tree, he turned his mind toward the Lord the way the sages had taught him, and for a moment the Lord appeared in his heart. Then it was gone. He tried and tried to see it again. A voice told him gently: you won't see me again in this life; I showed myself so your longing would grow. He spent the rest of that life singing the Lord's names, and was born again as Narada, who wanders the worlds with his vina. So the short book of sayings credited to Narada comes from someone who learned love the long way. The Narada Bhakti Sutras open like a manual: atha, now, then, we will explain bhakti. The second sutra gives the whole definition: toward this one, it is of the form of supreme love, parama prema. Commentators take this one to be the Lord. Then the sutras say what such love does. Having it, a person becomes complete and satisfied; they want nothing else, grieve for nothing, hate nothing. That's the teaching of bhakti: love for God so full that other wanting goes quiet. The word comes from bhaj, to share in, and to serve. And notice where Narada's love began: not in a temple, but in hearing stories near people who loved. That's still how many Hindus grow it, in satsang, good company, and kirtan, singing the names together.
screen: `ALONE, HE WALKS NORTH.` · `ONE GLIMPSE, THEN A VOICE.` · `ATHA: NOW, BHAKTI EXPLAINED.` · `PARAMA PREMA: SUPREME LOVE.` · then, large: `IT WANTS NOTHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, sing or hum one name of God you love, the way Narada did, a few times, slowly; if your family has a bhajan, use its first line. If you don't, bring to mind someone or something you love deeply. Then notice what the sutra describes: does the wanting quiet down a little? You don't need to make anything happen. Rest near what you love, and watch.
Bhakti. Devotion, from bhaj, to share and to serve. The Narada Bhakti Sutras call it supreme love.
